exp40v2-q.desk:
Desk Research and Secondary Sources

What public sources can settle, what they only reframe, and what they cannot touch at any price

1. Two decisions, six days apart

On Monday, 16 November 2026, Janaki Lavate had eighteen days. Lavate ran connected products at Jalsrot Filtration Industries, an Ahmedabad maker of reverse-osmosis purifiers with 4.6 lakh machines in homes across Gujarat and western Maharashtra. Her proposal was a subscription: a connected purifier installed free, filters replaced on sensor data rather than a calendar, ₹499 a month. The board would decide on 4 December on an ₹18 crore capital request, and Lalitha Kamerkar, the finance head, had set one condition — ₹22 crore of subscription revenue by the end of year three.

A Mumbai agency had quoted ₹52 lakh for 1,200 household interviews across six cities and eleven weeks of fieldwork. Eleven weeks did not exist. Kamerkar's question was blunter: before spending fifty-two lakh, what is already written down? Lavate assumed almost nothing was, and discovering how wrong that was changed her question rather than her estimate.

Three days later Janardhan Kesarkar faced the mirror image. Kesarkar ran product at Kritika Underwriting Systems, a Pune company whose underwriting workbench was used in part by twelve of the twenty-six motor underwriters in India. He wanted a motor-claims fraud module, reviewed on 10 December against a hurdle of ₹9 crore of recurring revenue by year three. His problem was abundance: the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India publishes segment premium by insurer, insurers file quarterly disclosures, four prospects are listed, and Latika Jogdand, his analyst, had assembled 140 pages with no way to say which page mattered.

Desk research is not a cheap substitute for primary research. It decides what primary research is for, and in the better case it dissolves the question the survey was to ask.

2. The idea, and who disagrees about it

Secondary data is gathered by someone else, for their purpose, and re-purposed for yours; primary data is gathered by you, to your specification. Desk research is the disciplined assembly, grading and reconciliation of secondary data into an answer a decision can rest on. In British commercial research of the 1950s the desk stage preceded the field stage as a matter of course.

Three lineages converge and disagree. Decision analysis, after Ronald Howard's formalisation of the value of information in the 1960s, holds that information is worth buying only if it can change what you do, and worth no more than the mistake it prevents times the chance of making it. It signs that no research should be commissioned before the decision, the threshold and the current estimate are written down; it refuses to sign that secondary data is generally adequate, the criterion being indifferent to provenance.

The estimation school, from strategy consulting and Fermi's habit of bounding unknowns by decomposition, signs that any commercially interesting quantity can be estimated from public data closely enough for a go/no-go decision, and that most disagreements between sources are definitional. It refuses to sign that estimates substitute for measured behaviour. The customer-development school signs that published categories are lagging artefacts, so sizing one guarantees you build inside it.

A fourth position deserves naming because the marketing-rooted programmes teach it: the panel school, built on concept tests, conjoint and continuous retail panels. The primary-secondary split is a false binary, it argues, since syndicated panel data is secondary in provenance and primary in rigour. It signs that for repeat-purchase goods a panel settles share and elasticity questions no filing can; it refuses to sign that a panel travels outside its measured universe, which in India under-covers kirana and the informal trade.

3. Mechanics in depth

Expert practice has six steps. The first and last are usually left implicit, and they separate a memo that changes a decision from a deck that decorates one.

One: write the decision, the threshold and the prior. Lavate's question was never how big the market was. It was whether to spend ₹18 crore against a ₹22 crore threshold — an unbounded brief turned into a single testable proposition.

Two: build a source ledger and grade every entry — who produced it, what it counts, and when the data was collected, which is almost never the publication date.

Table 1. Jalsrot's source ledger, 18 to 21 November 2026

Census and NSO tabulations2023-24Households by cityBoundaries lag build-out
Brokerage note on water treatmentMid-2026Installed base, service revenueTowards growth
Jalsrot's own service recordsRolling, 2024-26Service spend of ownersSurvivor bias

Three: estimate the quantity twice, by routes that share no ancestor.

The blended rate is not the mean of the column: it is 10.84 lakh divided by 48.5 lakh, or 22.35 per cent. The simple mean, 21.5 per cent, would overweight the small cities.

Three filters give the addressable set. Sixty-two per cent of the 10.84 lakh sit in pin codes Jalsrot can service within a day: 6.72 lakh. Of those, Jalsrot's records show 55 per cent out of warranty and paying for service — 3,69,644 households, the figure every later line uses. At the 12 per cent conversion Lavate assumed, 44,357 of those 3,69,644 households subscribe, which is 12 per cent, and at ₹499 a month, or ₹5,988 a year, that is ₹26.56 crore. Against a ₹22 crore hurdle the proposal clears by ₹4.56 crore.

Four: reconcile the routes and explain the gap. The brokerage note gave a national installed base of 1.85 crore households and an organised service-and-consumables market of ₹4,250 crore a year. Dividing one by the other gives the average annual service spend of an Indian purifier household, ₹2,297 — a figure that touches none of her bottom-up inputs, which is what makes it worth computing. It also detonates the proposal as framed, because Jalsrot was asking ₹5,988 a year, 2.6 times that.

The expert move is to finish the comparison rather than bury it. The subscription includes the machine, and a household buying outright pays about ₹12,000 every seven years — ₹1,714 a year of hardware it no longer funds. The honest reference spend is ₹2,297 plus ₹1,714, or ₹4,011, and ₹5,988 against ₹4,011 is a 49 per cent premium: large, but roughly a third as alarming as 2.6 times. Push once more. ₹2,297 is a national blend including small towns and unbranded machines; if the six cities run 1.35 times that average, their service spend is ₹3,101, the full reference ₹4,815, and the premium falls to 24 per cent. Three sources, no fieldwork, and the question has moved from how big the market is to whether a household will pay a 24 to 49 per cent premium for not thinking about filters.

Five: find the input that moves the answer. Lavate held the funnel fixed and varied the two things no public source records — conversion and price.

Table 3. Year-three revenue against the ₹22 crore hurdle

6%22,17913.2810.62

The annual fee is ₹5,988 at ₹499 a month and ₹4,788 at ₹399; no row is a total.

Six: write the residual list. The output is not a number but a ranked list of what remains unknown and what each unknown could do to the decision. Lavate's two entries interacted: the cheaper price needed the higher conversion. That is a two-arm price test on a few hundred households — ₹14 lakh rather than ₹52 lakh.

4. When it applies, and when it misleads

The quantity is a stock or flow somebody must report. Where this holds, desk research is close to decisive: motor premium by insurer is filed with a regulator, so Kesarkar's market size is a fact no survey could improve. Lavate's is half of this kind — households are counted, purifiers are not — so her base carries a real error band.

The published category matches what you are selling. Claims-fraud software appears in no filing, so Kesarkar must construct his market rather than look it up. Lavate's category exists but is defined around the transaction she wants to replace, so sizing it would measure the market she is leaving.

Behaviour under a new price or form is not the load-bearing unknown. Lavate fails this outright; her answer turns on a conversion rate and a price point that exist in no public source. Kesarkar passes: his buyers are twenty-six named firms he can ask.

The threshold is far from the estimate. If the threshold sits inside the error band, no amount of desk precision resolves it. Lavate's ₹22 crore sits between the ₹19.92 crore and ₹26.56 crore scenarios — the clearest possible signal to stop reading and start measuring.

The method is actively misleading where a regulatory or technological discontinuity means every published series describes the regime that is ending, and where the product creates its own category, so sizing adjacent ones imports their economics.

5. Hard edge cases

In two-sided markets public data sizes each side and says nothing about the join. Kalpavriksh Agri Exchange, a Nagpur produce platform, read 4.6 lakh tonnes of annual arrivals for its district cluster off public mandi data. What it could not show was that most of that volume was pre-committed to commission agents against crop advances: ninety farmer interviews costing ₹7 lakh found 63 per cent of arrivals pledged, leaving 1.70 lakh tonnes tradeable. The public figure answered a question about physical flow when the business question was contractual freedom.

In regulated markets the regulator publishes your market for you, and competitors read it too: Kritika's sizing is replicable in an afternoon, so advantage moves to interpretation and to the claims-handling detail only customers hold. In hardware-plus-software the bill of materials leaks through import data, certification registers and warranty provisions; Jalsrot's engineers could infer a rival's membrane supplier from its filings and its unit cost from disclosed margin and realisation. Cost structure says what a competitor can charge, not what it will.

In AI-native products no category exists, so the expert builds one from the cost line the product displaces. Lehja Voice Labs, selling voice agents for loan collections, found a listed non-banking lender disclosing ₹214 crore of collection and recovery expense against ₹18,600 crore of assets under management — 1.15 per cent of AUM. Applied to the twenty-two lenders disclosing a comparable line, with combined AUM of ₹3,84,000 crore, that implies ₹4,416 crore of annual collections spend; at 8 per cent capture, ₹353.3 crore. One borrowed ratio, whose weakest joint is whether it travels across books of different quality.

At the organisational seams, three failures recur: corporate strategy buys the analyst subscription and product does not know it exists; the research team holds panel data under a contract forbidding sharing; procurement holds competitor price lists nobody thinks of as research.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

Vintage is the fieldwork date

A competent practitioner checks that a report is recent; an expert reads the methodology annexe for when the data was collected. A 2026 report built on 2023 fieldwork describes a market three years gone. The tell is a document stating its publication date prominently and its fieldwork window in a footnote.

Three sources agreeing is often one source counted three times

The obvious reading is corroboration. The expert follows each citation to its origin and finds a chain. The tell is identical precision across documents: the same odd figure, to the same decimal, in three places that each cite the next.

Analyst reports are priced for investors

Their buyer wants a view on growth and tolerates loose levels, so their errors lean towards narrative. The expert reads the exit-year assumptions and ignores the headline. Lavate used the note only for two level figures, because those were what the analyst had least incentive to inflate.

Public data censuses the formal and gossips about the informal

Registration and tax thresholds create cliffs and distributions bunch below them, so the published size distribution of Indian small enterprises is partly an artefact of where the thresholds sit. The tell is a histogram spiking just under a round number; the obvious reading, that most firms are tiny, confuses reported with real turnover.

The best evidence is what the filer did not mean to disclose

Marketing language in an annual report is advertising; warranty provisions, segment-reporting changes and litigation notes are costly to state and therefore credible. When a competitor's warranty provision rises from 1.1 to 1.9 per cent of revenue a product broke, and no press release will say so. The expert reads filings backwards: notes first.

Absence of data points two ways

When a central quantity is published nowhere, either knowing it was never worth anything — so the market is smaller than it looks — or knowing it is an advantage incumbents guard, in which case the gap is the opportunity. The expert asks who would pay to know, and whether anyone is quietly selling it.

Desk research costs delay

Two weeks of a senior product manager is perhaps ₹1.2 lakh of salary and an unbounded amount of option value if a competitor is moving. The expert fixes a time box in advance — Lavate gave herself three days and five sources — and treats one more report as the signal to stop.

The usual output is a better question

The competent practitioner reports a market size; the expert reports that the market-size question was the wrong one. Lavate began by asking how many households were in the market and ended by asking whether they would pay a 24 to 49 per cent premium over current spend.

7. Across product types and stages

In consumer markets the data is abundant and contaminated, much of it published by people selling something, so the work is filtration. In B2B and enterprise the supply side is documented through filings while the buying process — who decides, against which budget line, on what cycle — is invisible, which is why Kesarkar can size his market to the rupee and not know whether anyone will sign this year. In platforms and marketplaces desk research yields a ceiling, never a forecast, because what matters is how much of each side transacts when the other is thin. In hardware and physical goods it is strongest: trade data, standards registers and realisation per tonne make competitors legible. In AI products the category does not exist and the method becomes ratio-borrowing from the displaced cost line, as at Lehja.

Stage changes less than people expect, and it is worth saying so plainly. The method is identical at seed and at scale; what changes is the alternative. An early company cannot afford fieldwork, so discipline about definitions is its only defence. A large one commissions fieldwork reflexively: Lavate's ₹52 lakh quote was 2.9 per cent of the ₹18 crore it was meant to protect, cheap enough that nobody asked what it would answer.

8. Three worked examples

Jigyasa Learning Network: a product killed for nothing

Jigyasa, a Bengaluru education company, considered a paid exam-preparation app for classes nine and ten in Hindi-medium private schools. Public enrolment statistics gave 2.18 crore students in those classes; the private unaided share was 36 per cent, or 78.48 lakh; consumption-survey tabulations put 22 per cent of those households above the income line at which ₹199 a month is plausible, or 17.27 lakh students once rounded. At the 4 per cent conversion its existing product achieved, that is 69,080 subscribers paying ₹2,388 a year: ₹16.50 crore, against an investment case requiring ₹40 crore. Two afternoons of arithmetic retired a proposal scheduled for a ₹30 lakh concept test.

Lauh Castings Industries: where it failed, and what recovery cost

In March 2023 Lauh Castings Industries, a Kolhapur foundry, read an industry report projecting Indian grey-iron castings exports to Europe rising from ₹8,400 crore to ₹13,100 crore in four years — about 11.8 per cent a year. It commissioned a ₹46 crore line of 14,000 tonnes annual capacity in September 2024, and by December 2025 was running 5,600 tonnes of the 14,000, or 40 per cent utilisation. The failure lay in reading the headline and not the annexe: ₹3,900 crore of the ₹4,700 crore projected increment — 83 per cent — sat in two tariff sub-headings for machined castings for wind-energy assemblies, needing a certification Lauh could not obtain inside two years. Its addressable slice was ₹800 crore of the ₹4,700 crore, 17 per cent of the increment. Recovery took nineteen months: re-specified for railway castings, the line reached 9,800 tonnes and 70 per cent utilisation by April 2026, after a ₹6.2 crore tooling write-off.

Kritika: desk research that settles quantity and exposes price

Kesarkar's sizing used only filings. Industry motor gross direct premium was ₹98,400 crore, allocated across the twenty-six underwriters by tier, with a contract value attached to each tier.

Table 4. Kritika's whole-market ceiling for the fraud module, built from regulatory filings
TierInsurersMotor GDP (₹ cr)ACV per insurer (₹ lakh)Module ARR if all adopt (₹ cr)
Top four private multiline434,8001807.20
Next eight private826,400957.60
Smaller private and specialist1013,600454.50
Public-sector insurers423,6001204.80
Total2698,40092.7 (blended)24.10

Blended ACV is ₹24.10 crore, or ₹2,410 lakh, divided by 26 insurers: ₹92.7 lakh. It is not the mean of the four tier figures, ₹110 lakh. Premium figures are illustrative but of the right order.

The ceiling is ₹24.10 crore if every insurer in India adopts. Kritika planned on 30 per cent of a ceiling in three years: ₹7.23 crore, short of the ₹9 crore hurdle by ₹1.77 crore. Desk research had answered the quantity question exactly and delivered a no.

Jogdand then rebuilt the case from the value side, again from filings. At a motor claims ratio of 79 per cent the industry incurs ₹77,736 crore of claims a year; published estimates of fraudulent and inflated motor claims cluster near 8 per cent of claims paid, or ₹6,218.88 crore. A module catching a tenth of that protects ₹621.9 crore, against which ₹24.10 crore of software revenue is 3.9 per cent of the value created. His ACV assumption, not his adoption assumption, was the error: lift every tier's ACV by 40 per cent and the ceiling is ₹33.74 crore, of which 30 per cent is ₹10.12 crore, which clears. The residual question became whether a second-tier chief underwriting officer would pay ₹133 lakh instead of ₹95 lakh.

9. Failure modes and their diagnostics

The headline-number memo. Early sign: one market size, no range. Diagnostic: name a second route sharing no source with the first.

Unit and definition drift. Early sign: a total an order of magnitude too large, usually because lakh and crore were mixed. Diagnostic: restate every figure in one unit and one definition.

An average from the wrong population. Early sign: a per-unit figure whose source population is richer than the target. Diagnostic: whose purchases were observed? Applying Lavate's national ₹2,297 to six prosperous cities understates their service spend by about a quarter.

Treating the desk phase as the answer. Early sign: a document ending in a number with no open questions. Diagnostic: what would we still have to learn from a customer? If nothing, capital gets spent on an estimate mistaken for a measurement.

Reading the headline, not the annexe. Lauh's failure, and the most expensive here. Early sign: a projection quoted without its segmentation. Diagnostic: where inside the total does the growth sit, and can you sell into that part?

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

The first disagreement is sequencing. The desk-first position rests on real evidence: most market-size disputes dissolve into definitional differences, and a practitioner who has not read the filings asks customers questions the filings already answer, wasting the scarcest resource in discovery. The field-first position holds that reading the published category corrupts the questions you then ask, and its evidence is anchoring: teams that size a category first propose products shaped like that category's. Sequencing depends on whether the decision is about capital allocation or product form.

The second concerns purchased panel data. The panel school holds that for repeat-purchase goods a panel settles share and elasticity questions no filing or survey can touch, and within its measured universe it is right. Its opponents point to coverage: a panel under-sampling small-format trade misstates exactly the segments where Indian growth happens. For the critics to be wrong, those gaps would have to be stable enough to adjust for.

The third is new and unsettled: whether a language model's synthesis of public sources counts as desk research. Advocates point to speed — a model reads Jogdand's 140 pages in minutes. Critics note that the discipline lives in provenance and vintage, and that synthesis untraceable to a fieldwork date reproduces Figure 3's citation chain at machine speed.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a thorough document. Someone who has internalised it writes the decision and its threshold before opening a source, so every hour is aimed; can say of any figure who collected it, when, and which way its error leans; treats agreement between sources as a claim requiring proof of independence; and ends the desk phase with a shorter list of sharper unknowns and a price on each.

12. The decisions

On 2 December Lavate took Kamerkar a four-page memo recommending neither the ₹52 lakh survey nor the ₹18 crore spend. It asked for ₹14 lakh and six weeks: a two-arm price test, ₹499 against ₹399, two hundred households per arm, run through Jalsrot's own service base, with capital released only if conversion exceeded 12 per cent at ₹499 or 15 per cent at ₹399. Desk research had fixed the quantity within a defensible band and identified, at no cost, the comparison that governed the outcome: ₹5,988 against a reference spend of ₹4,011 to ₹4,815.

On 10 December Kesarkar recommended building, with every tier's ACV lifted 40 per cent — ₹133 lakh rather than ₹95 lakh in the second tier — and commissioned no survey. He spent ₹6 lakh on eight conversations — four chief underwriting officers, two former claims heads, two loss adjusters — on one question: whether a leakage-sharing contract was procurable inside an Indian insurer's budget process. He entered them knowing the premium pool to the rupee, which is why each took forty minutes.

Discussion questions. First: if the brokerage's installed-base figure were overstated by a quarter, which of Lavate's conclusions would change and which would survive? Second: Kritika's sizing is replicable by any competitor in an afternoon, so what does Kesarkar gain from having done it, and where should his real advantage come from? Third: Lauh's report was accurate and its headline ruinous — what rule, applied to any projection, would have caught that before the ₹46 crore was committed?

13. Going deeper

Expert and analyst interviews. The residual list is best attacked by people who have watched the market from inside, and desk work makes those conversations short.

Survey design. How a residual question is asked decides whether the answer means anything; Lavate's price test is a design problem disguised as a pricing one.

Sampling and representativeness. Why 1,200 badly drawn households can be worse than a census you did not pay for.

Descriptive statistics for PMs. The blended-versus-mean distinction that separated ₹92.7 lakh from ₹110 lakh.

Conjoint and MaxDiff. The formal tool for the one thing desk research could never give Lavate: how households trade a fee against hardware.

Quantitative concept testing. How to measure response to a product form that does not yet exist.

NPS, CSAT and CES. Whether the subscription is holding, and when your own records become your best secondary source.
case20v1-q.desk:
Cobalt Charge and the Hyderabad Number

A decision case on desk research and secondary sources

1. Opening

On the evening of Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Sunita Kelkar sat in the glass-walled meeting room on the second floor of Cobalt Charge's head office in Baner, Pune, with two printouts in front of her. The first was a forty-page report on India's gig-mobility market from a global consultancy. The second was a one-page note from her finance head headed "Hyderabad: go or no-go?" The board of Cobalt Charge would meet on Friday, 6 November, two days before Diwali, and expected a recommendation on opening the company's second city.

Before that, Kelkar had to tell her team by Friday, 23 October which of three paths it would follow. She could commission a primary survey of delivery-fleet operators, which her research vendor in Mumbai had quoted at ₹24 lakh and ten weeks. She could spend two weeks and about ₹1.8 lakh of staff time reading everything public that bore on Hyderabad before spending anything on fieldwork. Or she could accept the consultancy's headline number, which looked favourable, and launch. She had not yet read her analyst's note on the report's methodology appendix.

2. Company background

Cobalt Charge was founded in Pune in 2021 by Kelkar, a former product manager at a two-wheeler manufacturer, and two engineers. The company runs battery-swap stations for electric two-wheelers ridden by delivery workers. A rider pays a monthly subscription of ₹1,800 and swaps a depleted battery for a charged one in under two minutes, which matters when each order is worth a few tens of rupees and a ten-minute charging stop is a lost delivery. Its customers are riders who work through fleet operators serving Zomato, Swiggy, Zepto and Flipkart's quick-commerce arm, and a smaller group of independent riders.

By September 2026 Cobalt had 38 stations in Pune and 3,400 paying subscribers, reached 26 months after the first station opened. The company employs about 140 people, with engineering in Pune and Bengaluru. Its competition is varied. Battery-swap specialists operate in several cities. Vehicle makers such as Ather and Ola Electric push their own charging networks and home chargers. Many fleet operators still run petrol bikes, because the up-front cost of an electric scooter remains a barrier even with state subsidies. Cobalt's position is narrow but defensible: it is the only operator in Pune whose stations are sited around dark-store clusters rather than main roads.

3. The situation

The board's interest in Hyderabad followed an investor visit in August. Hyderabad has a dense quick-commerce footprint, a state government that has advertised road-tax and registration waivers for electric vehicles, and a large population of delivery riders. Kelkar's team drafted a plan for 60 stations at ₹9 lakh each, a capital outlay of ₹5.4 crore, and monthly fixed costs of ₹48 lakh once running. At a contribution of ₹800 per subscriber per month after battery wear and electricity, break-even required 6,000 subscribers.

The consultancy report supplied the number that excited everyone: an estimated 1,80,000 active delivery riders in Hyderabad, against 1,10,000 in Pune. Sudhakar Kulshreshtha, the finance head, had applied Cobalt's Pune penetration to the larger city and drawn a conclusion that was close but, in his words, "uncomfortably close to the line". Others saw only that the market was larger.

The global team read it differently, and from where they sat. In Berlin, Stefan Kruger, who designs the swap cabinets, pointed out that Hyderabad's summer heat of over 40 degrees would affect battery temperature management, something no market report would tell them. In Singapore, Selina Kwok, who leads customer success, had noticed in Pune interviews that riders switched fleet operators every few months, so the subscriber base followed the operators, not the city's rider count. In Bengaluru, Kulshreshtha worried about spending cash that the next funding round might need. Each of them was reasoning from something public or something private, and none of them had yet separated the two.

4. The people

Sunita Kelkar, chief executive, Pune. She wants a decision she can defend to a board that includes two investors who have not seen a Cobalt station. She worries about spending ₹24 lakh to learn what a free report might already say, and equally about spending ₹5.4 crore on a number she cannot trace.

Sudhakar Kulshreshtha, finance head, Bengaluru. He built the break-even model. He wants a go decision only if the demand estimate clears 6,000 subscribers with margin, and he is wary of any plan that burns time through the festive season.

Selina Kwok, customer success lead, Singapore. She argues that retention among fleet riders is the real unknown and that no desk source speaks to it. She favours the survey, but with questions about switching behaviour.

Stefan Kruger, hardware designer, Berlin. He wants the climate and permitting facts established before any station is ordered, and he has little interest in the market-size debate.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 lists what Kelkar's analyst had gathered by the end of the first week and, more usefully, what each source actually measures. The last column matters most. None of the figures describes electric delivery riders in Hyderabad: the 1,80,000 count is Hyderabad's but covers riders of any vehicle, the 9 per cent was never measured in Hyderabad, and the 6 per cent is Hyderabad's but covers new registrations by all buyers.

Exhibit 2 sets out Kulshreshtha's arithmetic (lines D to G) alongside the analyst's electric-rider cases (lines B, C and H), with the base named for each line. Cobalt's Pune subscribers divided by Pune's 1,10,000 riders gives 3.09 per cent of all riders. Applying that to Hyderabad's 1,80,000 riders gives 5,564 subscribers, which is 436 short of the 6,000 break-even figure, a shortfall of 7.3 per cent. The same all-rider base is used in both cities, but the dates differ: the 3,400 subscribers are a 30 September 2026 count, while the 1,10,000 Pune riders are a June 2025 estimate, 15 months earlier. If Pune's rider count has grown since, the true Pune penetration is lower than 3.09 per cent and the Hyderabad projection is overstated. Nothing in the sources lets the team correct for this. Break-even in Hyderabad requires 3.33 per cent of all riders, against 3.09 per cent achieved in Pune after 26 months.

G. Shortfall (F − E)4367.3% of F
H. Break-even as share of line B / line C37.0% / 55.6%Share of electric riders Cobalt would need to win

Note: line H is shown for both electric-rider cases because the true Hyderabad electric share is unknown. 6,000 ÷ 16,200 = 37.0%; 6,000 ÷ 10,800 = 55.6%.

Exhibit 3. The three options compared
OptionCash spent before the go/no-goTime to answerWhat it can settle
A. Commission primary survey₹24 lakh10 weeks (1 January 2027)Rider and operator intent, switching behaviour
B. Two-week desk sprint₹1.8 lakh10 working days, 19 to 30 October (a week before the board)Which numbers hold, which bases are wrong, what to ask next
C. Launch on the headline number₹5.4 crore capexImmediateNothing; it tests the market by spending

Note: 60 stations × ₹9 lakh = ₹540 lakh = ₹5.4 crore. The ₹1.8 lakh in option B is internal staff time; it is not cash paid to a vendor.

6. The options

Option A: commission the survey now. The upside is direct evidence about the buyer. A well-designed survey of fleet operators could test willingness to pay ₹1,800 a month and how often riders move between fleets, which is precisely what Kwok fears. The cost is ₹24 lakh and a result on 1 January 2027, after the board has met and after the Diwali quick-commerce peak (Exhibit 3, and the timeline above). A survey also inherits whatever framing error is in the question; if the team does not know how many electric riders there are, it does not know whom to sample.

Option B: run a two-week desk sprint. The analyst and Kulshreshtha would trace every figure in Exhibit 1 to its base, pull the state electric-vehicle policy, read the Telangana transport department's circulars, check municipal and distribution-licence rules for swap stations, and mine two competitors' filings for station economics. The sprint would start on Monday 19 October, without waiting for the choice of path, and report on Friday 30 October, a week before the board. The cost is small. The limit is plain: public sources cannot say whether Hyderabad fleet operators would pay Cobalt's price, and a sprint that finds the numbers unsupported may leave the board with a "not yet" rather than a "no".

Option C: launch on the headline. The consultancy report is from a respected firm, the investor is keen, and the arithmetic in Exhibit 2 shows 5,564 subscribers against a need of 6,000, a shortfall that is small but still a shortfall. The upside is speed. The cost is ₹5.4 crore committed against a figure whose electric share was measured in other cities, and monthly fixed costs of ₹48 lakh that run whether or not riders arrive.

7. Questions for discussion

1. In Exhibit 1, which figures describe the population Cobalt wants to sell to, and which describe something adjacent? What would change if the 9 per cent were measured in Hyderabad rather than Bengaluru and Delhi NCR?

2. Exhibit 2 compares Hyderabad with Pune using all riders in both cities. Why is that comparison safer than applying Pune's share of electric riders, and what does the 436-subscriber shortfall actually tell Kelkar once the bases are admitted to be uncertain?

3. What can a desk sprint settle that a survey cannot, and the reverse? Using Exhibit 3, what is the cost of being wrong about each?

4. If you were Kelkar, what would you tell the team on 23 October, and what result from the first two weeks would change your mind before 6 November?

8. A note for the learner

Desk research answers a narrow question: what can be learned from sources that already exist before money is spent on fieldwork? Its value is not that public sources are accurate but that they are cheap and that they let a team find out which of its beliefs are borrowed. In this case the apparently solid number, 1,80,000 riders, is a consultancy estimate of riders on any vehicle, and the team has not checked it against anything; the number that would turn it into a market, the electric share, was measured in two other cities. The skill is to ask of every figure what population it covers, in which year, and whether a report has quietly applied it to a different one.

A well-reasoned answer separates three kinds of claim. Counts of riders are broad estimates that a consultancy can produce and that should be cross-checked against whatever the platforms disclose. Shares of electric vehicles are local and move fast; the registration dashboard shows new sales, not what is on the road, so it bounds the answer without giving it. Willingness to pay and switching behaviour are not public at all, and no amount of reading will substitute for asking the buyer.

One defensible path is Option B, with a rule fixed in advance. Run the desk sprint, and have the analyst trace Exhibit 1 line by line. Then decide: if public sources support an electric rider base near the high case, so that 6,000 subscribers is 37 per cent of electric riders rather than 56 per cent, break-even looks more attainable and the question becomes retention; note that line E still shows a 436-subscriber shortfall at Pune's penetration whichever case holds, so the high case makes the target plausible, not assured. The survey in Option A is then worth buying, narrowed to switching behaviour and scoped to the right sample. If sources point to the low case, the board is told that Hyderabad fails break-even unless Cobalt wins more than half of all electric delivery riders, and the plan is deferred. In either case, the desk work also feeds a short set of expert and analyst interviews, which is the natural next step in this module. Option C should be rejected not because the number is wrong, but because nobody on the team can yet say what it counts. Option A first would be defensible only if the sprint were impossible; here it is cheap and fast, and it makes the later survey better.
case40v1-q.desk:
Discovery & Design · Quantitative & Market Research · Case

Doorbeen Labs: The Number in Schedule 4

A product leader has twelve hours, two market models that differ by a factor of four, and a contract that defines the market for her.

1. The night before

On Sunday, 15 November 2026, the Diwali lights were still up on the compound wall of Tanushree Lotankar’s building in Koramangala, Bengaluru, three days after they should have come down. She had the balcony table, a cold cup of filter coffee and two documents open side by side on her laptop: a board pack she had signed off on Thursday, and a spreadsheet a colleague in Toronto had sent her on 22 October that she had been unable to argue away since.

At ten the next morning, 16 November, the investment committee of Doorbeen Labs Private Limited would decide whether to commit ₹14.4 crore over eighteen months to a general-trade product line — software for the small independent grocery store, the kirana, rather than for the supermarket aisles where the company had made its money. Tanushree, thirty-six, Senior Director of Product, owned the recommendation. Slide 6 of the pack carried a national market of ₹2,246 crore. The Toronto spreadsheet, rebuilt from public data, put the same national market at ₹513 crore.

Neither number came from a single customer conversation. Both were desk work: a subscription research report, a set of government releases, filings and investor decks, a purchased dataset of shelf audits, and a pilot of 212 stores designed to prove a thesis rather than test one. The committee would not ask where the numbers came from. It would ask whether she stood behind the recommendation, and the chief financial officer would ask what happened to the covenant if she did not.

What made the night uncomfortable was not that one number was wrong. It was that Tanushree could no longer tell which of the two measured the thing the company was about to buy.

2. Doorbeen Labs: a short history, and the clause of August 2024

Doorbeen Labs was founded in Bengaluru in March 2019 by Tushar Lagu, a former category manager at a national FMCG distributor, and Trivikram Lambe, a Pune engineer with six years on industrial vision systems. The product — Doorbeen Shelf — did one thing well: a salesperson photographed a shelf on a mid-range Android phone and the app returned share-of-shelf, planogram compliance and out-of-stock flags for every stock-keeping unit in the frame. Brands paid for the audit; retailers got the report free.

The early customers were consumer companies of the kind that publish their general-trade and modern-trade mix in quarterly investor presentations — the Maricos, Daburs and Hindustan Unilevers of the Indian market — and their regional distributors. Growth came from modern trade because modern trade was legible: Reliance Retail, Avenue Supermarts’ DMart and Spencer’s had store masters, planograms and a single point of negotiation. By FY2026 revenue was ₹61.8 crore (Exhibit 1), with engineering in Bengaluru and Pune, design in Berlin, data science in Toronto, customer success in Singapore and sales in Newark, New Jersey.

The decision that constrains November 2026 was taken in August 2024. Dhanuk Growth Partners invested ₹90 crore for a minority stake at a ₹540 crore pre-money valuation. The money bought eighteen months of runway and the Berlin and Toronto hires. It also bought a milestone: ₹18 crore of annual recurring revenue from general trade by 31 March 2028, failing which Dhanuk’s ratchet resets the Series A2 conversion price and Tushar and Trivikram together give up a further 4.1 per cent of the company.

The clause that nobody argued about at the time was the definition. Schedule 4 of the subscription agreement defines “general trade” by reference to the outlet taxonomy published in Darpan Advisory Services’ India Retail Digitisation Outlook — the report Doorbeen had been quoting in fundraising decks since 2023, and to which it pays ₹14 lakh a year for a three-seat licence. Doorbeen did not write the definition of its own target market. It subscribed to it.

3. The industry

Indian retail in 2026 was two businesses pretending to be one. Modern trade and quick commerce — Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Blinkit, Tata’s BigBasket, Reliance’s JioMart — were capital-rich and instrumented, and every cohort chart was in a filing or an investor call. General trade was the rest: millions of counter-service shops with a ledger, a Paytm or PhonePe QR code and an inventory that lived in the owner’s head. UPI had put a payment rail into those shops, and NPCI’s monthly statistics were the single most reliable series anyone had about them.

The regulatory surface was real but not hostile. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 mattered because a shelf photograph occasionally contains a customer’s face, and Doorbeen’s on-device blur had been built for that reason. GST had incidentally created the most useful public register of trade India had ever had: GSTN taxpayer counts by state and activity code let anyone count registered retail entities without asking a single shopkeeper. The limitation was definitional — a registration is not a shop, one registration may cover several outlets, and most kiranas fall below the threshold at which registration is compulsory.

Doorbeen’s exposure was not only Indian. Its second market was the Gulf, where Dalaan Hypermarkets, a Dubai group with 118 supermarkets and a franchised network of 1,400 small groceries across the UAE, had been a customer since January 2022 and was now 18.4 per cent of company revenue through a single contract. Tian Loke in Singapore carried that account; Tyler Lanigan in New Jersey carried a nascent North American pipeline at salary bands four times Bengaluru’s. Every rupee committed to kirana software in Nagpur was a rupee not committed to a renewal in Dubai, and everyone in the room on Monday knew it.

4. The situation in detail

The general-trade thesis entered Doorbeen’s plan in February 2025, when Tushar renewed the Darpan licence and asked the strategy analyst to size the opportunity “the way Dhanuk will size it”. The build is Exhibit 2, and it took an afternoon: 1.3 crore retail outlets in India, of which 18 per cent judged digitally addressable, at an average revenue per store of ₹9,600 a year, giving ₹2,246 crore. Twelve cities were taken to hold 28 per cent of addressable outlets, giving a serviceable market of ₹629 crore, of which a 4 per cent share in three years would be ₹25.2 crore of annual revenue in FY2029. Nobody at the time observed that the Schedule 4 test falls a year earlier, on 31 March 2028, and is measured as ARR rather than as revenue. The slide went into the August 2024 data room retrospectively, into the FY2026 operating plan, and in March 2026 into an appendix submitted to Doorbeen’s bankers in support of a ₹25 crore working-capital line.

What was believed in February 2025 was that the hard part was engineering: a kirana shelf is cluttered, badly lit and deeper than it is wide, and models trained on modern-trade planograms failed on it. So Doorbeen bought data. In June 2025 it licensed three years of historical merchandiser audit labels from Doab Distribution Services, a distributor in central and western India, for ₹2.6 crore — 1.9 lakh shop photographs, each already scored for compliance by Doab’s field staff. Accuracy against those labels reached 94 per cent by March 2026 and the module was declared technically ready.

The pilot ran from 10 September to 31 October 2026 in Nagpur, Indore and Coimbatore: 212 stores, all introduced by Doab’s area sales managers. The results were the best numbers anyone at Doorbeen had seen. 184 of the 212 pilot stores (86.8 per cent) moved on to a paid tier at the end of the free window, at a blended ₹365 per store per month — ₹299 for the base plan plus ₹66 of average add-ons — against a list price of ₹499 — ₹8.06 lakh of annualised subscription value in total, a figure that appears nowhere in the pack. Tanushree put the conversion rate on slide 9 and did not put the two facts beside it: the stores were selected by a distributor who earns a trail commission on each subscription, and the window straddled the pre-Diwali loading weeks, when a kirana’s stock turn and a brand’s merchandising spend are both at their annual peak. Diwali fell on 8 November in 2026; the stores had been measured at the top of their year.

Three things have since turned out to be wrong, or at least unsafe. First, on 22 October, Tegan Lefebvre, who had joined in Toronto in July and had been asked to “re-derive the GT number so the board sees a bottom-up view”, delivered the first version of Exhibit 3: a chain running from the urban population projection and the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey down to 11.7 lakh included outlets, which at the ₹499 list price gave a national market of ₹701.7 crore. On 9 November, once the pilot’s paid conversions were known, she revised that line to the blended ₹365 the stores had actually signed, and the national figure fell to ₹513.2 crore — 22.8 per cent of the ₹2,246.4 crore on slide 6, which is the only comparison of the two that is national against national. Second, on 4 November, a re-audit of 420 pilot photographs by Doorbeen’s own two trained auditors returned a Cohen’s kappa of 0.45 against the purchased Doab labels (Exhibit 4), which is to say that the dataset the models had been trained and scored against was a moderately reliable opinion rather than ground truth. Third, on 7 November, Tegan traced Darpan’s ₹9,600 average revenue per store back to its origin: a single willingness-to-pay question in Darpan’s metro panel, answered by 146 shopkeepers, none of whom was a general-trade kirana (Exhibit 5).

Tanushree closed the board pack on Thursday 12 November with slide 6 unchanged. On the afternoon of Friday 13 November she asked Trishala Limaye whether the lender appendix could be amended without re-opening the covenant. Trishala replied, by message, with one word: “Why?”

5. The people

Tanushree Lotankar — Senior Director, Product (Bengaluru)

Owns the recommendation and has carried the GT thesis in every plan since FY2026. Her stated position is that the direction is right and only the size is in doubt, so the company should commit and learn. Her incentive is uncomfortable: the GT line is the reason her remit was expanded and two of her four product managers were hired. What she is not saying is that she had read Darpan’s methodology note in August and knew then that the ₹9,600 figure was a stated-preference median from a metro modern-trade panel, and chose not to flag it before the plan was locked; what she did not know until 7 November was that it rested on 146 answers.

Tushar Lagu — co-founder and chief executive (Mumbai)

Wants the full ₹14.4 crore committed on Monday and the Nagpur pilot extended to six cities before the March quarter. His argument is that Indian distribution is won by whoever is in the lane first, and that every month of analysis is a month of a competitor’s head start. His incentive is Schedule 4 and the 4.1 per cent. What he is not saying is that he has already told Dhanuk’s partner, verbally, on a call on 3 November, that GT ARR would cross ₹6 crore in FY2028, and that he has no memory of which model that number came from.

Trishala Limaye — chief financial officer (Mumbai)

Position: stage-gate the spend at ₹3.6 crore for two quarters, with a hard review in April 2027. She is the only person in the company who reads the term sheet and the banking documents in the same sitting, and she is unmoved by TAM arguments of any size. What she is not saying is that the ₹2,246 crore slide is an annexure to the lender submission of March 2026, that the facility carries a plan-adherence covenant, and that she has not yet worked out whether a downward restatement of the market is a disclosure event or merely an embarrassment.

Tegan Lefebvre — staff data scientist (Toronto)

Built Exhibit 3 and believes it. Position: no further spend until a probability-sampled store study exists, because every number the company owns is either a vendor’s or a volunteer’s. Her incentive is intellectual: she has twice offered to present the reconstruction internally as a worked example of source triangulation. What she is not saying is that only 11 of the 28 states in her sample frame carry observed per-outlet throughput; the remaining 17 are imputed from a regression on state urbanisation, and the summary tab of her model does not mention it.

Tilda Lemke — design lead (Berlin)

Position: before another rupee goes into the model, send researchers into forty shops for a fortnight, because the pilot measured subscription behaviour under distributor pressure and not shopkeeper need. She is the only voice in the company for primary qualitative work. Her incentive is that a field programme protects the two contract researchers she has on a rolling budget. What she is not saying is that her team has never run a study in India, that she would need to hire local moderators in three languages, and that the quote she has in hand covers Nagpur alone.

Tian Loke — head of customer success (Singapore)

Position: the ₹14.4 crore belongs in the Gulf, where a known buyer is asking for a product. He notes, correctly, that Dalaan is ₹11.4 crore of the ₹18.6 crore Gulf line, or 61 per cent, and renews on 31 March 2027. His incentive is a retention bonus above 92 per cent gross revenue retention. What he is not saying is that Dalaan’s procurement has twice asked for a data-residency commitment he cannot make, and that this, not the roadmap, is the live risk to the renewal.

Tyler Lanigan — vice-president, sales, North America (Newark, New Jersey)

Position: India general trade is a ₹365-a-month business and North American enterprise retail a ₹40,000-a-month business, so the committee is debating the wrong continent. He quotes a qualified pipeline of ₹48.3 crore. His incentive is a quota missed for three consecutive quarters. What he is not saying is that the figure is the gross sum of open CRM opportunities, that ₹19.5 crore of it is one prospect logged twice under two legal entities, and that ₹6.4 crore is past its close date (Exhibit 6B).

Taimur Lalchandani — category director, Dalaan Hypermarkets (Dubai)

Wants the general-trade module, but for Dalaan’s 1,400 franchised baqalas in the UAE, and offers ₹4.2 crore of co-funding against twenty-four months of GCC exclusivity. His incentive is a digitisation commitment he made to his own board for 2027. What he is not saying is that he is in parallel conversation with a European vendor, and that the “19 per cent uplift in on-shelf availability” he cites comes from a GCC-wide modern-grocery study whose sample held no franchised small-format stores at all.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

“Tegan’s number is beautiful work and a number nobody will fund. Dhanuk did not put ₹90 crore into a ₹513 crore market. If we restate on Monday we are not having a strategy discussion, we are having a governance discussion.”

Tushar Lagu, voice note to Tanushree, 13 November 2026, 11:42 p.m. IST

“I have not shown that the market is small. I have shown that the ₹2,246 crore cannot be built from any population we can name. Those are different claims and I would like the minutes to record the second one.”

Tegan Lefebvre, model review call, 9 November 2026 (08:30 Toronto, 19:00 Bengaluru)

“We have spent ₹2.6 crore on a distributor’s opinion of what a tidy shelf looks like, ₹14 lakh a year on a report whose author will not show us her screener, and ₹0 on walking into a Nagpur shop to ask a man why he says yes to the salesman in October, and what he will do when the first invoice reaches him in February.”

Tilda Lemke, design review, 6 November 2026

“I have 1,400 baqalas and a board paper due in January. The GCC study shows 19 per cent uplift in on-shelf availability. If Doorbeen cannot build the small-format module by June I must look at the Rotterdam people, and I would rather not.”

Taimur Lalchandani, Dalaan Hypermarkets, e-mail, 12 November 2026

“Renewal risk is not a roadmap problem. Taimur wants the module, but procurement wants to know where the photographs are stored. That is the conversation that decides ₹11.4 crore, and it is not on Monday’s agenda.”

Tian Loke, internal chat thread #gulf-renewals, 14 November 2026

“Two questions for the committee. First, which number is in the lender annexure. Second, which number we will be quoting in April if the April number is different again. I can live with either model. I cannot live with a company that has three.”

Trishala Limaye, e-mail to Tushar Lagu and Tanushree Lotankar, 14 November 2026

“We trained on Doab’s labels because they were there and cheap at the margin. I never claimed they were truth. I claimed they were consistent. Kappa of 0.45 says they are not even that.”

Trivikram Lambe, engineering note circulated 4 November 2026

8. The options as Tanushree sees them

Option one: commit, and keep slide 6. Approve the full ₹14.4 crore, extend the pilot to six cities, and leave the Darpan build in the pack on the grounds that it is the definition the contract uses anyway. The attraction is speed and internal peace. The cost is a company managing to a market it no longer believes in, with the next re-derivation of the number coming from a diligence analyst in a Series C data room rather than a colleague in Toronto.

Option two: commit at a quarter of the size. Take Trishala’s stage gate: ₹3.6 crore — 25 per cent of the programme — over two quarters, a hard review in April 2027, with the gate defined on paying stores outside the Doab-introduced set. The attraction is that it buys evidence cheaply. The cost is that a two-quarter gate ending in April measures stores through January and February, the slowest months of a kirana’s year, as the pilot measured them through the fastest — and a gate whose base is seasonally wrong can kill a good product as easily as a bad one.

Option three: buy primary data before committing. Commission a probability-sampled store study: 900 stores, 30 clusters of 30, six cities, ten weeks, ₹68 lakh. On a proportion near one half, a simple random sample of 900 gives a 95 per cent interval of about ±3.3 percentage points; with a design effect of 1.6 the effective sample is 562 and the interval widens to about ±4.1 points. It is the only option that produces a number Doorbeen owns. The cost is ten weeks, and the committee sits on Monday morning.

Option four: take Dubai’s money and build the small-format module for the Gulf first. Taimur’s ₹4.2 crore covers 29 per cent of the programme, leaving ₹10.2 crore — 71 per cent of it — on Doorbeen’s own books, and gives a named buyer. The attraction is commercial discipline. The cost is twenty-four months of GCC exclusivity, a module shaped by franchised baqalas rather than Indian kiranas, and nothing at all for Schedule 4, which is defined over Indian general trade.

Tanushree had written these four on a card. What she had also written, and crossed out, was a fifth line: none of the above is a research decision. The four options all assume that the question is how much to spend and where. They do not touch the possibility that the company’s problem is a definition it rented, or that the cheapest useful work available before Monday — reading what the listed FMCG companies say about general-trade growth in their own filings, pulling GSTN activity-code counts state by state, downloading two years of NPCI merchant-transaction data, and asking Doab for the labelling protocol it has twice declined to send — costs nothing and had not been done.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The investment committee meets at 10:00 a.m. IST on Monday, 16 November 2026, with Dhanuk’s observer dialling in from Singapore. The FY2028 Schedule 4 milestone is ₹18 crore of general-trade ARR by 31 March 2028, defined on the Darpan taxonomy, with a conversion-price ratchet and 4.1 per cent of founder equity attached. The working-capital facility of ₹25 crore carries a plan-adherence covenant and was supported in March 2026 by an annexure containing the ₹2,246 crore build. Cash stood at ₹58.8 crore on 31 October 2026 against a monthly net burn of ₹2.23 crore on the H1 average, with the proposed programme adding ₹0.8 crore a month. October alone ran at ₹2.4 crore, which would give 24.5 months rather than 26; Trishala uses the six-month average on the grounds that October carried the licence prepayments, and nobody has tested that claim. The Doab data licence runs to June 2028 and is non-cancellable; the Darpan licence renews on 1 February 2027 at ₹14 lakh.

Engineering capacity binds: Trivikram has nineteen engineers across Bengaluru and Pune, six of them committed to the Gulf data-residency work that Tian says will decide the Dalaan renewal. Taimur’s co-funding offer lapses on 30 November, a probability-sampled study cannot deliver before late January, and the Berlin field programme needs moderators in Marathi, Hindi and Tamil whom Tilda has not yet identified.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Trace the ₹2,246 crore of Exhibit 2 back to the populations it was measured on. Which multiplications are defensible, and which change the population, the year or the geography mid-stream?
  2. Exhibit 5 reports that 68.2 per cent of those asked would pay for shelf analytics. What is the right denominator for Doorbeen’s purpose, and what would you do with the ₹800 median if you had to use it at all?
  3. Exhibit 4 gives a kappa of 0.45 on a dataset that cost ₹2.6 crore and on which the production models were trained and scored. What exactly does that invalidate, and what does it leave standing?
  4. Exhibit 3 is built from public sources and is not therefore more trustworthy than Exhibit 2. Name the assumptions on which it turns, and say what each would cost to test.
  5. Doorbeen’s definition of its own market was written by a research firm it pays, and now sits in a term sheet and a lender annexure. What should a product leader do about that — and at what point does correcting a market estimate become a governance act rather than an analytical one?
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Tanushree recommend, what does she stop doing, and what does she say to the board about a number the board has been quoting for twenty-one months?

Near midnight, Tanushree did one more thing before closing the laptop. She opened the Darpan report to page 118, read the methodology note again, and then opened the annual report of a listed consumer company she had never thought to look at, because its general-trade revenue per outlet was printed there, audited, for two years running. The figure matched neither model. She wrote it on the card below the crossed-out line, looked at the three numbers for a while, and did not decide anything.

The Diwali lights on the compound wall were still burning when she went in.
exp20v2-q.desk:
Desk Research and Secondary Sources

What can be learned from public sources before any money is spent on primary research

1. The proposal on the table

On Tuesday, 3 November 2026, Sunanda Tiwarekar, a senior product manager at Tarkeeb Packaging Industries, a corrugated-box manufacturer with plants near Pune and Coimbatore, received a message from her finance head. A proposal had been drafted for the board meeting on 24 November: build a procurement marketplace on which small manufacturers could order packaging from several approved converters, with Tarkeeb as the anchor supplier and the platform's operator. The build budget was ₹4.2 crore. The board wanted evidence that the market was large enough.

A research agency had already quoted ₹38 lakh for a survey of 400 buyers, with a fieldwork window of nine weeks. Uday Soman, the sales director, thought the survey was the only honest route: "Nobody has written down what a Nashik food processor pays for cartons. We would be guessing." Tahlia Sutherland, a marketplace consultant engaged from Melbourne, disagreed: most of it already sat in public registries, filings and trade reports, and a survey should answer only what those could not.

Tiwarekar had fourteen days. If she recommended the survey and the answer proved to be knowable for nothing, the company would burn ₹38 lakh and two months. If she skipped it and the public numbers misled her, the board might commit ₹4.2 crore to a market half the size she had claimed. The crux: how far could she trust what others had already published?

2. The idea

Desk research is the practice of answering a business question using information that already exists: government registries, company filings, trade-association reports, analyst notes, academic papers and press coverage. Such material is called secondary data, because it was collected by someone else for a purpose other than yours. Primary data is what you gather yourself, through surveys, interviews or experiments, designed around your question. A filing is a document a company is legally obliged to submit to a regulator, such as the annual report of a listed firm or the financial statements an unlisted company lodges with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs.

The method grew out of the mid-twentieth-century commercial research industry, when firms such as A. C. Nielsen sold standardised market data. Its modern importance comes from economics: public data, such as India's Udyam registration portal and the Annual Survey of Industries, became free to find, while fieldwork stayed expensive.

The sentence Tiwarekar could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: "Public sources tell us how big the room is and who is already in it; only customers can tell us whether they would walk through our door." Desk research decides what primary research must ask, and whether it is needed at all.

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have five steps, and practitioners usually leave the first and last implicit. The first is to write the decision before the question. Tiwarekar's decision was whether to commission a survey, and the board's threshold was explicit: the marketplace needed a realistic revenue ceiling above ₹60 crore a year, taking a commission of 2 per cent of the packaging spend that flowed through it. That threshold turned "how big is the market" into "is annual spend through our reachable buyers above ₹3,000 crore?", since 2 per cent of ₹3,000 crore is ₹60 crore.

The second step is to list candidate sources and weigh each. Weighing means asking who produced the number, why, how recently and by what method. Tiwarekar's inventory is in Table 1.

Table 1. Source inventory for the packaging question
SourceTypeVintageWhat it can tell herMain risk
Udyam registry counts by industry codeGovernment registryUpdated monthlyNumber of manufacturing units by sectorRegistered is not active; sizes are self-declared
Trade-association packaging reportIndustry bodyPublished in 2025Total corrugated market and share by buyer typeMembers fund it; tends to flatter the sector
Annual reports of two listed packaging makersStatutory filingsYear to March 2026Realised price per tonne and customer mixLarge-buyer bias; excludes small units

The third step is to build the estimate by two independent routes. A top-down estimate starts from a large published total and carves it down by shares. A bottom-up estimate starts from units and unit spend and multiplies up. If the routes land close together the agreement is evidence; if they diverge, the gap is information. The fourth step is to explain every difference, and the fifth, usually omitted, is to write down what remains unknown and who could answer it. That list is the real product.

4. A worked example

Tiwarekar took four buyer segments from the Udyam registry and priced each unit's yearly corrugated spend from the two listed makers' disclosures of tonnage and realisation, adjusted for typical order sizes. Table 2 shows the bottom-up build. Each row's annual spend is units multiplied by average spend per unit, converted at 100 lakh to a crore.

Units sum to 101,000. The average spend per unit is total spend divided by total units: 3,58,300 lakh divided by 1,01,000 is about ₹3.55 lakh, not the simple mean of the four row averages.

The top-down route used the trade association's report: a corrugated market of ₹21,000 crore, of which 18 per cent was bought directly by small and medium manufacturers. Eighteen per cent of ₹21,000 crore is ₹3,780 crore. The bottom-up figure of ₹3,583 crore is ₹197 crore lower, which is 5.2 per cent below the top-down figure. Two independent routes agreeing within about five per cent is reassuring, and both clear the board's ₹3,000 crore threshold. At a 2 per cent commission, the revenue ceiling is ₹71.7 crore against the ₹60 crore hurdle.

Now the second pass, which is where the learning happens. Sutherland asked how the food-processing average of ₹3.2 lakh had been derived. It turned out to rest on the two listed makers' customer disclosures, and those makers sell mainly to larger food companies. A small Nashik unit would plausibly buy less. Suppose the true average is ₹2.4 lakh. Food processing then falls to 42,000 times 2.4, which is 1,00,800 lakh, a drop of 33,600 lakh from the first pass. The new total is 3,58,300 minus 33,600, or 3,24,700 lakh, which is ₹3,247 crore, and the average spend per unit falls to about ₹3.21 lakh.

The new bottom-up figure is ₹533 crore below the top-down figure, a gap of 14.1 per cent. The revenue ceiling at 2 per cent becomes ₹64.9 crore. The threshold is still cleared, but the margin has narrowed from about ₹11.7 crore to about ₹4.9 crore. One input moved, and the picture went from "comfortable" to "marginal". Desk research gives an answer with a known dependency, here one segment's average spend, which a small targeted survey can measure.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

Secondary is not second-rate, and primary is not automatically truer

People assume that numbers gathered for you must be better than numbers gathered for someone else. A badly sampled survey of 400 buyers can be less reliable than a government census of every registered unit. What matters is fit and method, not provenance.

Who paid for the report decides what the report says

The trade association's figure of ₹21,000 crore comes from a body whose members sell corrugated boxes. It has no motive to understate. Incentives do not make a source false, but they show which way its errors lean.

Definitions differ silently between sources

One report counts "MSME" by investment in plant, another by turnover, a third by employees. A registry may count a unit once per registration, so a firm with two plants can appear twice. Most large discrepancies turn out to be definitional rather than factual.

Triangulation is evidence only if the routes are independent

If both routes quietly depend on the same underlying report, their agreement is an illusion. Had Tiwarekar derived unit spend from the trade report, she would have been checking a number against itself.

Desk research cannot measure intent or unmet need

Public data records what was bought, not what buyers wished they could buy, nor why they chose a supplier. It cannot say whether a Nashik purchase manager would trust an unfamiliar platform.

Questions to ask before relying on a number

Who produced it, and who paid? What exactly is counted, and for which period? What would have to be true for it to be wrong by a third?

6. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, desk research is rich but crowded, and the difficulty is separating signal from marketing. In B2B products such as Tarkeeb's, registries and filings give the supply side well, but the buying process, who actually decides and how, is invisible in public data. In marketplaces, the hardest quantities are two-sided: public sources size supply and demand separately but say almost nothing about whether each side will join when the other is thin. A marketplace estimate from desk research is therefore a ceiling, never a forecast.

Stage matters too. An early-stage company often cannot afford fieldwork, so its discipline about definitions matters more. A large company risks the opposite failure: commissioning a survey out of habit when its own sales records and public filings already hold the answer. Tarkeeb sits between: the survey's ₹38 lakh is about 9 per cent of the ₹4.2 crore build it would protect, which is sensible insurance only if it addresses a real open question.

7. Common mistakes

Quoting a single headline number. The symptom is a slide with one market-size figure and no range. The misunderstanding is that a published number is a measurement rather than an estimate. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask the author for a second route to the same quantity; if none exists, the number is a hypothesis.

Mixing units and definitions. The symptom is a total that is suspiciously large, often because lakh and crore, or turnover and investment bands, were combined. The underlying error is treating every table as comparable. The diagnostic is to rewrite every figure in one unit and one definition before adding anything.

Averaging up from the wrong population. Tiwarekar's own first pass did this: the large-buyer average was applied to small buyers. The diagnostic is to ask of each average, "whose purchases were observed?"

Treating the desk phase as the answer. The symptom is a report that ends with a market size and no list of open questions. The misunderstanding is that the purpose is a number. The diagnostic is to ask, "what would we still need to learn from a customer?" If the answer is "nothing", the desk work has overreached.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled version of Tiwarekar's fortnight would produce a four-page memo. It would state the decision and the ₹3,000 crore threshold on page one. It would present a source table like Table 1, two estimates reconciled with the gap explained, and a sensitivity run like the second pass, showing which single input moves the answer most. It would close with a short list of residual questions, ranked by how much each could change the decision. It would cost almost nothing and tell the board what to buy next.

9. The decision, and what to learn next

On 17 November, fourteen days after the first message, Tiwarekar recommended against the full ₹38 lakh survey. She proposed instead a narrow study of 60 small food-processing buyers, the segment whose average spend most affected the answer, along with six conversations with procurement managers to test willingness to use a shared platform. Desk research had settled the size of the room to within a defensible band; it could not settle the one input that mattered or the behavioural question no registry records. She also asked the board to approve the build only on the condition that the narrow study confirmed an average food-sector spend of at least ₹2.4 lakh.

The natural next topic is expert and analyst interviews, because the residual questions desk research leaves behind are usually best answered by people who have seen the market from inside. Desk work tells you whom to interview and what to ask; the interviews then tell you whether the public numbers deserve the trust you gave them.

Two questions to sit with. First, think of a market-size figure you have recently relied on: can you name a second, independent route to it, and what would a gap of 14 per cent between the two routes have told you? Second, which single input in your own current estimate, if wrong by a third, would change your decision, and have you checked it?
